overview: MIN is a SQL aggregate function that returns the smallest value in a column or expression across the rows in scope.
It works not only on numbers but also on strings (ordered by the column's collation) and on dates/timestamps (returning the earliest), and like other aggregates it ignores NULLs.
MIN is commonly paired with GROUP BY to find the smallest value per group, and with correlated subqueries to retrieve the earliest record per entity.
learningObjectives: Understand how MIN finds the smallest value across numeric, string, and date/time types.
Master MIN's NULL-ignoring semantics and how collation affects MIN on strings.
Apply MIN with GROUP BY and correlated subqueries to fetch per-group earliest records, and understand index usage.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: MIN(expression) is an aggregate function that returns the minimum (smallest by the data type's ordering) non-NULL value of the expression over the rows in scope — the entire result set or each GROUP BY partition. For numbers it is the lowest number; for strings it is the first value by collation/sort order; for dates/timestamps it is the earliest. MIN ignores NULL values entirely, and returns NULL only if every value in scope is NULL or there are no rows.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: MIN looks through all the values in a column and hands you back the smallest one. 'Smallest' means lowest number for numbers, earliest date for dates, and first-in-sort-order for text. If some cells are empty (NULL), MIN just skips them — it will never return NULL unless every value is NULL.
coreConcept.historicalContext: MIN, along with MAX, COUNT, SUM, and AVG, is one of the original aggregate functions in the SQL-86 standard derived from Codd's relational algebra. Its NULL-ignoring behavior and reliance on the type's collation/ordering were formalized in ANSI/ISO SQL and are consistent across PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, and cloud warehouses, making MIN one of the most portable functions in SQL.

whyItMatters.business: MIN answers fundamental business questions: the lowest price offered, the first time a customer transacted, the earliest event in a session, or the minimum stock level triggering a reorder. These drive pricing, retention, and inventory decisions.
whyItMatters.engineering: MIN underpins 'earliest record' and 'floor value' logic throughout ETL and analytics. Understanding its NULL and collation behavior is essential to build correct cohort, funnel, and SLA calculations.
whyItMatters.scalability: MIN is a single-pass, mergeable aggregate that scales to billions of rows and parallelizes trivially, since partial minimums per partition combine into a global minimum.
whyItMatters.cost: When backed by an ascending index, MIN can be answered by reading a single index entry instead of scanning the table, dramatically reducing I/O and query cost in pay-per-scan systems.
whyItMatters.reliability: Because MIN feeds 'first seen' and 'lowest value' metrics that gate alerts and business rules, understanding its exact semantics (NULL handling, collation) keeps those rules dependable.

coreComponents.name: The Compared Expression
coreComponents.definition: The column or expression whose smallest value MIN returns, e.g. MIN(price) or MIN(order_date).
coreComponents.purpose: Defines the values being compared and the data type that determines the ordering used.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Must be of an orderable type (numeric, string, date/time); non-NULL values are compared by that type's ordering.

coreComponents.name: Type-Specific Ordering
coreComponents.definition: The ordering rule MIN uses: numeric order for numbers, collation order for strings, chronological order for dates/timestamps.
coreComponents.purpose: Determines what 'smallest' means; for strings this depends on the column's collation (case sensitivity, locale).
coreComponents.responsibilities: Governs comparison; e.g. case-insensitive collation treats 'a' and 'A' as equal for ordering.
coreComponents.examples: MIN over ('Banana','apple') depends on collation; MIN over dates returns earliest

coreComponents.name: GROUP BY / Correlated Subquery Context
coreComponents.definition: The scoping mechanism — GROUP BY partitions, or a correlated subquery — that lets MIN run per entity rather than over the whole table.
coreComponents.purpose: Finds the smallest value per group (e.g., earliest order per customer) and supports per-group earliest-record retrieval.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Defines the partition over which the minimum is computed.
coreComponents.examples: SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id

internalWorking: The engine scans rows in scope, evaluating the expression for each row and skipping rows where it is NULL.
It maintains a single running 'current minimum'; each non-NULL value that is smaller than the current minimum replaces it, using the data type's comparison/collation rules.
If a usable ascending index exists on the column, the optimizer may skip the scan and read the first (lowest) index entry directly — an index-only min lookup.
After processing all rows (or each group), it emits the running minimum; if no non-NULL value was seen, it returns NULL without error.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Rows in scope -> evaluate expression per row -> skip NULLs -> compare each value to running minimum (by type ordering) -> keep the smaller -> emit one minimum per group (or one overall)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. Engine reads order_date values for customer 42: 2023-05-10, NULL, 2023-01-02, 2023-03-15.
3. Running minimum starts at 2023-05-10, then 2023-01-02 is smaller and becomes the new minimum, then 2023-03-15 is larger and is ignored.
4. MIN(order_date) returns 2023-01-02 — the customer's earliest order.

keyTerminology.meaning: The set of rules that defines string ordering and comparison (case sensitivity, accents, locale).
keyTerminology.importance: MIN over strings depends entirely on collation; the same data can yield different minimums under different collations.

keyTerminology.meaning: The row with the minimum timestamp per entity, found via MIN(timestamp) grouped by the entity.
keyTerminology.importance: A staple pattern for cohort analysis, first-purchase attribution, and onboarding funnels.

keyTerminology.meaning: Answering MIN by reading the first entry of an ascending B-tree index instead of scanning the table.
keyTerminology.importance: Turns an O(n) scan into an O(log n)/O(1) lookup, a major performance optimization.

importantConcepts.explanation: MIN excludes NULL values from comparison and returns NULL only when there are no non-NULL values. This means a column full of values plus some NULLs returns the smallest actual value, not NULL.

importantConcepts.concept: MIN value vs the whole earliest row
importantConcepts.explanation: MIN(order_date) returns only the date, not the rest of that order's columns. To get the entire earliest row per group you need a correlated subquery, a window function (ROW_NUMBER), or a join back on the min value.

variationsAndTypes: **MIN on numbers:** Returns the lowest numeric value.
**MIN on strings:** Returns the first value by collation order (locale/case-sensitivity dependent).
**MIN on dates/timestamps:** Returns the earliest point in time.
**MIN with GROUP BY:** Returns the smallest value per group.
**Windowed MIN (MIN(col) OVER (...)):** Returns the running/partitioned minimum without collapsing rows.
advantages: **Type-agnostic:** Works on numbers, strings, and dates with consistent, standard semantics.
**NULL-safe:** Skips NULLs so it surfaces the smallest real value rather than NULL.
**Index-accelerable:** Can be answered from an ascending index without a full scan.
**Mergeable:** Partial minimums combine, so it parallelizes and scales effortlessly.
disadvantages: **Returns only the value, not the row:** Getting the full earliest record requires extra logic (subquery/window).
**Collation surprises on strings:** The 'minimum' string can vary by collation, confusing case-sensitivity expectations.
**NULL-only groups return NULL:** May require COALESCE for presentation.
**Outlier sensitivity for floors:** A single erroneous low value can dominate MIN, masking the typical floor.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use MIN to find the smallest/earliest value — lowest price, first event, minimum threshold — especially with GROUP BY for per-entity floors and first-seen timestamps, and when an ascending index makes it nearly free.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid MIN alone when you need the entire earliest row (use ROW_NUMBER/correlated subquery), or when a single anomalous low value would mislead — then prefer a low percentile or filtered minimum.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Think of scanning a shelf of milk cartons to grab the one with the earliest expiry date. You glance at each printed date, ignore any carton with a smudged/missing date (NULL), and keep track of the earliest date you've seen so far. At the end you pick that carton — that is exactly what MIN does over a date column.

commonMisconceptions.myth: MIN returns NULL if any value in the column is NULL.
commonMisconceptions.reality: MIN ignores NULLs and returns the smallest non-NULL value. It returns NULL only when every value is NULL or the group is empty.

commonMisconceptions.myth: MIN(date) gives you the whole earliest row.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It returns only the minimum date value. To retrieve all columns of the earliest row you need a correlated subquery, a self-join on the min, or a window function like ROW_NUMBER.

productionConsiderations.scalability: MIN is mergeable: each partition/shard computes a local minimum and the coordinator takes the minimum of those, so it scales linearly and parallelizes cleanly across distributed engines.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Reliability depends on consistent collation for string minimums and clear NULL semantics. Pin collation explicitly when MIN over text feeds business logic to avoid environment-dependent results.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: MIN is recomputable from source data and idempotent, so failed aggregation jobs simply re-run. Incremental rollups can store per-bucket minimums that merge correctly after partial failures.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Monitor first-seen minimums for unexpected backward jumps (a new earlier record) or NULL results (empty groups), which often signal upstream data issues or late-arriving historical data.
productionConsiderations.security: A MIN over a small or single-row group can reveal an individual's value (e.g., earliest visit). Apply minimum-group-size thresholds for privacy-sensitive minimums.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Create an ascending index on columns frequently used with MIN so the engine answers via index lookup instead of full scans, cutting I/O and cost.
productionConsiderations.performance: MIN is fastest with a B-tree index ordered ascending on the column (and on the GROUP BY key for per-group minimums). Without an index it requires a full scan of the relevant rows.

codeExamples.title: MIN across numbers, strings, and dates (with NULLs)
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrates that MIN works on multiple types and ignores NULLs.
codeExamples.code:
-- products: price (numeric, one NULL), name (text), launched_on (date)
-- prices: 9.99, NULL, 4.50, 19.00
-- names:  'Zeta','apple','Beta'
-- dates:  2022-06-01, 2021-12-31, 2023-01-15

SELECT
    MIN(price)        AS cheapest_price,    -- 4.50 (NULL ignored)
    MIN(name)         AS first_name_sorted, -- depends on collation
    MIN(launched_on)  AS earliest_launch    -- 2021-12-31
FROM products;
codeExamples.breakdown: MIN(price) returns 4.50, skipping the NULL row entirely. MIN(name) returns the first name in collation order — under a case-sensitive ASCII collation uppercase letters sort before lowercase, so 'Beta' or 'Zeta' may precede 'apple'; under a case-insensitive collation 'apple' would come first. MIN(launched_on) returns the earliest date, 2021-12-31.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: cheapest_price=4.50, first_name_sorted depends on collation (e.g., 'Beta' under case-sensitive, 'apple' under case-insensitive), earliest_launch=2021-12-31
codeExamples.commonIssues: Expecting MIN to return NULL because a NULL exists; assuming string MIN is always case-insensitive; forgetting collation differences across environments.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Pin the collation explicitly (e.g., MIN(name COLLATE ...)) when string ordering feeds business logic, so results are reproducible.

codeExamples.title: MIN with GROUP BY: earliest order date per customer
codeExamples.overview: Finds each customer's first-purchase date and counts how many have no orders.
codeExamples.code:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    MIN(order_date) AS first_order_date,
    COUNT(*)        AS total_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY first_order_date;
codeExamples.breakdown: GROUP BY customer_id partitions the orders so MIN(order_date) returns the earliest order per customer — the classic first-purchase / acquisition-date metric. Any customer rows with a NULL order_date are skipped by MIN; a customer whose orders all have NULL dates would yield NULL first_order_date.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: One row per customer with their earliest order_date and order count, ordered by first_order_date.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Putting non-aggregated columns in SELECT without adding them to GROUP BY; assuming MIN returns the rest of that earliest order's columns (it does not).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Add a composite index on (customer_id, order_date) so the per-group minimum is served efficiently from the index.

codeExamples.title: Per-group earliest full row via correlated subquery
codeExamples.overview: Retrieves the entire earliest order row per customer, not just the min date.
codeExamples.code:
SELECT o.*
FROM orders o
WHERE o.order_date = (
    SELECT MIN(o2.order_date)
    FROM orders o2
    WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id
);

-- Equivalent, often faster, window-function approach:
-- SELECT * FROM (
--   SELECT o.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
--       PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date ASC
--   ) AS rn
--   FROM orders o
-- ) t WHERE rn = 1;
codeExamples.breakdown: The correlated subquery computes MIN(order_date) for each customer and the outer query returns every order whose date matches that minimum, giving the full earliest row(s). If two orders share the earliest date you get both; ROW_NUMBER with a tiebreaker returns exactly one. The window-function version is usually more efficient because it scans the table once instead of re-evaluating the subquery per row.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The complete columns of each customer's earliest order; ties on the min date return multiple rows in the subquery version.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Ties on the minimum date returning multiple rows unexpectedly; correlated subquery performing poorly on large tables due to repeated evaluation.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Prefer ROW_NUMBER for large datasets; add a deterministic tiebreaker (e.g., ORDER BY order_date, order_id) to guarantee a single row per group.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A subscription company wants to build acquisition cohorts based on each customer's first-ever order date, and noticed that some customers were missing from cohorts because a few orders had NULL order dates from a legacy import.
endToEndExample.inputData: An orders table (order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount) where order_date is occasionally NULL due to a historical data-migration gap.
endToEndExample.architecture: A relational/analytics warehouse with an orders fact table indexed on (customer_id, order_date), queried by a cohorting job that buckets customers by first-order month.
processingSteps: 1. Compute MIN(order_date) per customer with GROUP BY customer_id to get each customer's first-purchase date.
2. Recognize that MIN skips NULL order_date rows automatically, so customers with at least one dated order still get a valid first date.
3. Flag customers whose first_order_date is NULL (all their orders had NULL dates) for data-quality remediation rather than dropping them silently.
4. Derive the acquisition month with DATE_TRUNC('month', first_order_date) to assign each customer to a cohort.
5. Aggregate counts and revenue per cohort month for retention analysis.
endToEndExample.output: A per-customer first_order_date plus a cohort_month, and a separate list of customers with NULL first_order_date needing data fixes.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Track the count of customers with NULL first_order_date over time; a rise indicates new ingestion gaps. Watch for first dates moving earlier, which signals late-arriving historical orders.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Customers whose first_order_date is NULL are routed to a remediation queue (not assigned to a cohort) so the legacy NULL dates can be backfilled rather than corrupting cohort metrics.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Accurate acquisition cohorts where each dated customer lands in the correct first-purchase month, NULL-date customers are surfaced for cleanup instead of silently lost, and the (customer_id, order_date) index keeps the per-customer MIN fast.

industryUseCases.company: Retail and inventory systems (e.g., Walmart, Target)
industryUseCases.problem: Identifying the lowest current price across suppliers per SKU and detecting items below a minimum stock threshold for reorder.
industryUseCases.solution: MIN(price) GROUP BY sku finds the cheapest supplier offer; MIN(stock_level) flags items at or below reorder points.
industryUseCases.benefits: Competitive pricing and timely replenishment, with NULL/unavailable supplier prices ignored automatically.

industryUseCases.company: Product analytics / growth teams (e.g., Spotify, Duolingo)
industryUseCases.problem: Determining each user's first activity date for acquisition cohorts and onboarding funnels.
industryUseCases.solution: MIN(event_timestamp) GROUP BY user_id yields the first-seen timestamp, feeding cohort and retention analysis.
industryUseCases.benefits: Correct cohorting and funnel attribution; users with sparse/NULL early events still get a valid first-seen value.

industryUseCases.company: Logistics and SLA monitoring (e.g., FedEx, DHL)
industryUseCases.problem: Finding the earliest scan event per shipment and the minimum transit time per lane for SLA baselines.
industryUseCases.solution: MIN(scan_time) GROUP BY shipment_id locates the first scan; MIN(transit_hours) GROUP BY lane sets the best-case baseline.
industryUseCases.benefits: Accurate first-touch timing and best-case SLA baselines that ignore missing scan data.

productionDeepDive.scalability: MIN is a distributive aggregate: each shard/partition computes a local minimum and the coordinator takes the minimum of those, giving linear scaling and natural parallelism across distributed query engines and MapReduce-style frameworks.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: MIN is idempotent and recomputable from source rows, so failed jobs re-run safely. Persisting per-bucket minimums in rollups lets partial results merge correctly after failures.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Read replicas serve MIN queries deterministically; replica lag affects only freshness. Hot 'first-seen'/'lowest price' values can be cached with short TTLs.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: After a restore, minimums recompute trivially from the underlying data. Index rebuilds restore the ascending index that accelerates MIN lookups.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Create an ascending B-tree index on the MIN column (and a composite index on (group_key, min_col) for per-group minimums) so the optimizer can do an index-only lookup. Filter with WHERE before aggregating and use columnar storage to scan only the needed column.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Index-backed MIN reads a single index entry instead of scanning the table, slashing I/O cost in scan-billed warehouses. Maintain incremental per-bucket minimums to avoid rescanning raw data.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Minimums over tiny groups can disclose individual values (e.g., a single user's first visit). Enforce minimum group sizes and consider masking for sensitive first-seen data.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Alert on MIN results that unexpectedly move earlier (late-arriving history) or become NULL (empty/all-NULL groups). Track NULL ratios in the MIN column as a data-quality signal.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate the MIN column's type and collation are as expected. Assert that newly computed minimums are not earlier than a plausible business epoch to catch corrupt/placeholder dates.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log the collation and filter used for string minimums so results are auditable. Alert when first-seen minimums regress unexpectedly, indicating backfills or bad timestamps.

recommendedPractices: **Index for MIN:** Add an ascending index on columns frequently used with MIN to enable index-only lookups.
**Pin collation for string MIN:** Specify collation explicitly when the smallest string drives business logic, for reproducible results.
**Use window functions for full earliest rows:** Prefer ROW_NUMBER over correlated subqueries to fetch the entire earliest record at scale.
**Handle NULL-only groups:** COALESCE NULL minimums to a clear sentinel/label rather than displaying NULL silently.
engineeringStandards: Per-group earliest-row queries must include a deterministic tiebreaker to return a single row.
String MIN used in business rules must declare its collation.
Columns used with MIN in hot queries must be backed by an appropriate ascending or composite index.
designRecommendations: Store per-entity first-seen minimums in a derived dimension/rollup to avoid recomputing over the full fact table.
Use composite indexes on (group_key, min_col) for per-group minimums.
When you need the whole earliest row, design the query with ROW_NUMBER PARTITION BY group ORDER BY min_col.
namingConventions: Name minimum columns with a min_ or first_ prefix and the unit, e.g. min_price, first_order_date.
Distinguish per-group minimums clearly, e.g. earliest_event_per_user.
documentationStandards: Document the collation used for any string MIN.
Document the NULL-handling expectation (skip vs sentinel) for the minimum.
Document the tiebreaker chosen for earliest-row queries.
testingStrategies: Test MIN against fixtures containing NULLs to confirm NULLs are skipped and only an all-NULL group returns NULL.
Test string MIN under the target collation to lock in expected ordering.
Test earliest-row queries with tied minimum values to verify the tiebreaker returns exactly one row.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming MIN returns NULL when the column contains any NULLs.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers conflate NULL presence with NULL output, not realizing aggregates skip NULLs.
commonMistakes.impact: Misdiagnosed queries and unnecessary COALESCE/filters; sometimes wrong logic built around a non-existent NULL result.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Remember MIN ignores NULLs and returns the smallest non-NULL value; it is NULL only for all-NULL/empty groups.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting MIN(date) to also return the rest of the earliest row's columns.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Aggregates return a single scalar per group, but the desire is the full record.
commonMistakes.impact: Selecting other columns alongside MIN without GROUP BY errors or returns arbitrary/incorrect values.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY col) = 1, or a correlated subquery matching the MIN, to fetch the whole earliest row.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring collation when taking MIN of strings.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Collation is invisible until results differ across environments (case-sensitive vs insensitive, locale).
commonMistakes.impact: The 'minimum' string varies between databases/configs, causing inconsistent business logic.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Specify the collation explicitly when string ordering matters, e.g. MIN(name COLLATE "C") or the appropriate locale collation.

comparisonSection.feature: Getting the earliest value vs the earliest full row
comparisonSection.optionB: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY col) = 1
comparisonSection.explanation: MIN(col) returns only the smallest scalar value per group. ROW_NUMBER (or a correlated subquery on the MIN) returns the entire earliest row with all columns, and with a tiebreaker guarantees exactly one row per group.

comparisonSection.feature: Performance of finding the smallest value
comparisonSection.explanation: With an ascending B-tree index the optimizer reads the first index entry — an O(log n)/O(1) index-only lookup. Without an index, MIN must scan all relevant rows, an O(n) operation that is far slower and costlier on large tables.

The smallest string can differ: case-sensitive ASCII collations sort uppercase before lowercase (so 'Z' < 'a'), while case-insensitive collations compare letters regardless of case. Pin the collation to make MIN over text deterministic.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does MIN do, and which data types does it work on?
beginnerQuestions.answer: MIN returns the smallest value in a column or expression. It works on numbers (lowest number), strings (first by collation order), and dates/timestamps (earliest). It ignores NULL values.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Show breadth across types and immediately mention NULL-skipping, since both are common follow-ups.

beginnerQuestions.question: Does MIN return NULL if some rows are NULL?
beginnerQuestions.answer: No. MIN ignores NULLs and returns the smallest non-NULL value. It returns NULL only when every value in scope is NULL or there are no rows.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: This dispels the most common beginner misconception about MIN.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you find the earliest order date for each customer, and how would you get the full earliest order row?
intermediateQuestions.answer: For the date: SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id. For the full row, MIN alone is not enough — use a window function: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) and keep rn = 1, or a correlated subquery where order_date = (SELECT MIN(order_date) ... WHERE same customer).
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate the distinction between the min value and the min row, and mention tiebreakers for deterministic single-row results.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does collation affect MIN on string columns?
intermediateQuestions.answer: MIN on strings returns the first value by the column's collation. A case-sensitive ASCII collation sorts uppercase before lowercase (so 'Zoo' could be less than 'apple'), while a case-insensitive collation ignores case. The same data can yield different minimums under different collations, so pin the collation when it matters.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Knowing collation impact signals real-world experience with cross-environment inconsistencies.

advancedQuestions.question: How can MIN be answered without scanning the whole table, and when does that optimization apply?
advancedQuestions.answer: If there is an ascending B-tree index on the column, the optimizer can perform an index-only lookup, reading just the first (lowest) index entry instead of scanning all rows. For per-group minimums, a composite index on (group_key, min_col) lets the engine seek the minimum within each group efficiently. The optimization applies for plain MIN(col) (and grouped MIN) but is defeated by functions/expressions on the column that the index cannot satisfy.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Mention the index structure, the per-group composite-index case, and that wrapping the column in a non-indexed expression disables the shortcut.

advancedQuestions.question: Write a query for the earliest record per group that returns exactly one row even with ties on the minimum.
advancedQuestions.answer: Use ROW_NUMBER with a deterministic tiebreaker: SELECT * FROM (SELECT o.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC) AS rn FROM orders o) t WHERE rn = 1. The order_id tiebreaker guarantees a single row when two orders share the minimum date.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Contrast with the correlated-subquery-on-MIN approach, which returns multiple rows on ties; the tiebreaker is the key insight.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A report of 'first login date per user' suddenly shows many users with a NULL first login, even though they clearly logged in. What do you investigate?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: MIN returns NULL only when all values in the group are NULL. So those users' login_timestamp must be NULL for every one of their rows — likely an ingestion or schema change nulled the timestamp, or the join is bringing in rows from a table where the timestamp is absent. Check the NULL ratio of login_timestamp per affected user and whether a recent pipeline change altered the column.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: The NULL first-login values mean those users have no non-NULL login_timestamp at all — investigate an upstream change that started writing NULL timestamps or a faulty join. MIN itself is behaving correctly; the data feeding it is the problem.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a system that serves 'first-seen timestamp per user' for hundreds of millions of users with low-latency reads.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Maintain a first_seen dimension table keyed by user_id holding MIN(event_timestamp). Update it incrementally: for each new event, set first_seen = LEAST(existing_first_seen, new_timestamp). Back the events table with an index on (user_id, event_timestamp) for any recomputation. Serve reads directly from the small first_seen table.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Incrementally maintaining first_seen with LEAST avoids rescanning all events but requires careful handling of late-arriving (earlier) events, which must move first_seen backward. Storing the derived minimum trades a little write complexity for very fast reads.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Shard by user_id; each shard computes and stores its users' minimums independently. Use the (user_id, event_timestamp) index for index-only MIN during backfills and parallelize per shard.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: MIN returns the smallest non-NULL value of a column, by numeric order (numbers), collation (strings), or chronology (dates).
keyConcepts: MIN ignores NULLs; returns NULL only for all-NULL/empty groups.
Works on numbers, strings (collation), and dates (earliest).
Returns only the value, not the whole row.
Ascending index enables an index-only MIN lookup.
Pair with GROUP BY for per-group minimums.
formulas: N/A — MIN is a comparison-based aggregate, not a numeric formula.
Full earliest row: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY col) = 1
commands: SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
SELECT * FROM (SELECT o.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) rn FROM orders o) t WHERE rn = 1;
interviewPoints: MIN ignores NULLs (returns NULL only if all NULL).
Use ROW_NUMBER/subquery for the full earliest row.
Ascending index gives index-only MIN lookups.
Add a tiebreaker to handle ties on the minimum.
quickNotes: MIN, like SUM/AVG/MAX, skips NULLs per the SQL standard.
MIN(date) returns the earliest date but not the rest of that row.
An ascending B-tree index turns MIN into a fast index lookup; expressions on the column can disable it.
String MIN depends on collation; pin it for reproducible results.
For per-group earliest full rows, ROW_NUMBER with a tiebreaker is preferred over correlated subqueries at scale.

keyTakeaways: MIN returns the smallest non-NULL value and works across numbers (lowest), strings (first by collation), and dates (earliest), ignoring NULLs unless the whole group is NULL.
MIN returns only the value, not the full earliest row — use ROW_NUMBER() or a correlated subquery (with a tiebreaker) to retrieve the entire record.
An ascending B-tree index lets the optimizer answer MIN with an index-only lookup instead of a full scan, and composite indexes accelerate per-group minimums.
String minimums depend on collation, so pin the collation when the smallest string drives business logic to keep results reproducible across environments.
MIN is a mergeable, idempotent aggregate that scales and parallelizes trivially and can be maintained incrementally with LEAST(old_min, new_value).
